s: Radio frequencies from about 3 to 30 MHz (the HF range), which can travel thousands of kilometres by bouncing off the ionosphere.
b:
Shortwave is the common name for the high-frequency (HF) radio range, roughly 3–30 MHz. Broadcasters also use the 2.3–2.5 MHz 120 m band, so receivers usually tune from about 1.7 MHz upward.

Shortwave signals reflect off the ionosphere and return to Earth far from the transmitter. One transmitter can reach listeners on another continent with no satellites or internet involved. That is why international broadcasters, time stations, aircraft, ships and amateur operators still use it.

s: Someone who listens to shortwave radio without transmitting.
b:
SWL stands for shortwave listener: anyone who tunes the HF bands to receive broadcasts, utility signals or amateur stations, without transmitting. No licence is needed to listen in most countries.

Many SWLs keep a log of what they hear and send reception reports to stations to collect QSL cards.

s: Hearing distant or hard-to-receive stations; DXing is the hobby of chasing them.
b:
DX is old telegraph shorthand for distance. In radio it means a distant or difficult station, and DXing means deliberately hunting for signals that are weak, rare or far away.

Shortwave DXers chase low-power stations, rare transmitter sites and brief openings near the grey line. AM (mediumwave) DX is the same hobby on 530–1700 kHz after dark.

s: A card or letter from a station confirming that you heard its broadcast.
b:
A QSL card is a station's written confirmation of your reception. The name comes from the Q-code QSL, meaning "I acknowledge receipt".

To get one, send the station a reception report with the date, UTC time, frequency, programme details and a signal rating such as SINPO. Some broadcasters still mail printed cards; many now reply by email with an eQSL.

s: A listener's report to a station describing what was heard, when and how well.
b:
A reception report tells a station that its signal reached you. A useful report lists the date and time in UTC, the frequency, your location, your receiver and antenna, a signal rating (often SINPO) and enough programme detail to prove you heard it.

Stations use these reports to check coverage, and many reply with a QSL card.

s: A five-figure code that rates Signal, Interference, Noise, Propagation and Overall quality from 1 to 5.
b:
SINPO is a standard way to rate shortwave reception. Each letter gets a score from 1 (worst) to 5 (best): Signal strength, Interference from other stations, Noise (static and electrical noise), Propagation disturbance (fading) and an Overall rating.

A clear, strong signal might be 54454; a weak, noisy one 23332. Be honest: stations value an accurate 2 more than a hopeful 5. The simpler SIO code uses only Signal, Interference and Overall.

s: The world time standard used by every shortwave schedule.
b:
UTC is the time reference used by broadcasters worldwide, so one schedule works in every country. It does not change for daylight saving time. For everyday listening, UTC is the same as GMT.

To convert, add your offset: US Eastern is UTC−5 in winter and UTC−4 in summer; UK is UTC+0 in winter and UTC+1 in summer. Schedules also write times like 2000z or 2000 UTC.

s: A free, regularly updated database of world shortwave broadcast schedules.
b:
EIBI is a free shortwave schedule database compiled by Eike Bierwirth. It lists frequency, UTC times, station, language, target area and transmitter site for broadcasters worldwide, and is updated throughout each broadcast season.

ShortwaveHQ rebuilds its station, frequency and band pages from the EIBI data every day.

s: The High Frequency Coordination Conference, where broadcasters coordinate shortwave frequency use each season.
b:
The HFCC is an association of international broadcasters and transmission operators. Before each broadcast season, members file their planned frequencies, times and target areas so collisions can be found and resolved.

HFCC publishes the coordinated schedule as public data files. ShortwaveHQ uses them to cross-check EIBI listings and to build its next-season preview.

s: The two shortwave scheduling periods each year: A (summer, from late March) and B (winter, from late October).
b:
International broadcasters change schedules twice a year to follow daylight saving time and shifting propagation. The A season starts on the last Sunday of March; the B season starts on the last Sunday of October. Seasons are written with the year, such as A-26 or B-26.

In the first days of a new season many stations move frequencies or times, so schedules are worth rechecking.

s: A named shortwave broadcast band, such as 31 m (9.4–9.9 MHz), identified by its approximate wavelength.
b:
Broadcasters cluster in allocated ranges called meter bands, named for their approximate wavelength: 49 m around 6 MHz, 41 m around 7 MHz, 31 m around 9.5 MHz, 25 m around 11.8 MHz, 19 m around 15.4 MHz and so on.

Lower bands (60–41 m) work best at night; higher bands (19–13 m) work best in daylight. Wavelength in metres is roughly 300 divided by the frequency in MHz.

s: Units of frequency: 1 MHz = 1,000 kHz. Shortwave schedules usually give frequencies in kHz.
b:
Frequency is measured in hertz (cycles per second). One kilohertz (kHz) is 1,000 Hz; one megahertz (MHz) is 1,000 kHz. So 9,730 kHz and 9.730 MHz are the same frequency.

Most shortwave schedules use kHz. Radios differ in what they display, so be ready to move the decimal point.

s: How radio signals travel from transmitter to receiver, including reflection from the ionosphere.
b:
Propagation describes the path a signal takes. On shortwave the key mechanism is skywave: refraction in the ionosphere brings signals back to Earth hundreds or thousands of kilometres away.

Conditions depend on time of day, season, the sunspot cycle and geomagnetic activity. Indicators such as the solar flux index and K-index help predict them.

s: A signal that reaches the receiver after being refracted back to Earth by the ionosphere.
b:
Skywave is the long-distance path that makes shortwave work. The signal leaves the antenna at an upward angle, is bent back by the ionosphere and lands far away. A signal can make several of these hops.

Between the end of ground wave coverage and the first skywave landing point lies the skip zone, where nothing is heard.

s: A signal that travels along the Earth's surface, giving short-range coverage.
b:
Ground wave follows the curve of the Earth. It is strong at low frequencies, which is why longwave and AM stations cover a region reliably by day, and weak on shortwave, where it fades out within tens of kilometres.

Beyond ground-wave range, shortwave relies on skywave.

s: The electrically charged upper atmosphere (about 60–1000 km up) that bends shortwave signals back to Earth.
b:
Sunlight ionises gases in the upper atmosphere, forming layers that refract radio waves. The D layer (lowest) absorbs lower frequencies in daytime and disappears at night. The E layer reflects some signals. The F layer (split into F1 and F2 by day) does most of the long-distance work.

Because the layers follow the Sun, propagation changes through the day, through the seasons and across the 11-year sunspot cycle.

s: The highest frequency that the ionosphere will return to Earth on a given path at a given time.
b:
Above the MUF, signals pass through the ionosphere into space. Below it they come back down. The MUF rises during the day and with higher solar activity, which is why the 19 m to 13 m bands open in daytime and in sunspot-cycle peaks.

The best frequencies are usually a little below the MUF.

s: The lowest frequency usable on a path before ionospheric absorption makes signals too weak.
b: The LUF is set mainly by absorption in the D layer, which is strongest around midday. Below the LUF, signals are absorbed before they can make the trip. At night the D layer fades, the LUF drops and lower bands such as 49 m and 41 m open up.

s: A daily measure of the Sun's radio output at 10.7 cm, used as a proxy for ionisation and HF conditions.
b:
The solar flux index is measured at 2800 MHz (10.7 cm wavelength). Low values (around 70) mean a quiet Sun and lower MUFs. Higher values (130 and up) mean more ionisation and better conditions on the higher shortwave bands.

SFI says nothing about disturbances; check the K-index for that.

s: A 0–9 scale of geomagnetic disturbance over the past three hours; lower is better for shortwave.
b:
The K-index measures how disturbed Earth's magnetic field is. 0–2 is quiet and good for listening. 3–4 is unsettled. 5 and above is a geomagnetic storm, which can weaken or black out paths, especially those crossing polar regions.

The planetary Kp index combines readings from observatories worldwide.

s: A daily average of geomagnetic activity derived from the K-index; lower values mean steadier conditions.
b: The A-index summarises a full day of geomagnetic activity on a linear scale. Values below about 10 are quiet; above about 30 indicates storm conditions. It changes more slowly than the K-index and is useful for spotting multi-day trends.

s: The roughly 11-year rise and fall of solar activity that drives long-term shortwave conditions.
b: Solar activity swings from minimum to maximum and back about every 11 years. Near solar maximum, the ionosphere is more strongly ionised, MUFs are higher and the upper shortwave bands open widely. Near minimum, the high bands are often quiet and the lower bands carry most traffic.

s: The band around the Earth where it is sunrise or sunset, often bringing unusually good long-distance reception.
b:
The grey line, or terminator, divides day from night. Along it, the absorbing D layer has faded on the dark side while the higher layers are still ionised, so signals can travel far with little loss. Paths that run along the grey line can open briefly to distant stations.

Listening around your local sunrise and sunset is a classic DX technique.

s: The area between ground-wave range and the first skywave landing point, where a signal cannot be heard.
b: A shortwave signal can be inaudible a few hundred kilometres from the transmitter yet strong much farther away. The gap is the skip zone. Its size grows with frequency: higher bands skip farther.

s: Rises and falls in signal strength caused by changing ionospheric paths.
b:
Shortwave signals often arrive by more than one path, and the paths change constantly. When they add, the signal strengthens; when they cancel, it fades. Selective fading hits parts of the signal unevenly and causes distortion on AM.

Synchronous detection and ECSS tuning reduce fading distortion.

s: The mode most shortwave broadcasters use: audio varies the strength of a carrier signal.
b:
In AM, the audio changes the amplitude of a carrier wave, producing two sidebands that carry the same audio. Any shortwave radio can receive it, which is why international broadcasters still use it.

AM is vulnerable to fading and noise. Synchronous detection improves it.

s: A mode that transmits only one sideband with no carrier; it needs an SSB-capable receiver.
b:
Single sideband removes the carrier and one sideband from an AM signal, saving power and spectrum. Amateur operators, aircraft, ships and many utility stations use it. Upper sideband (USB) and lower sideband (LSB) are the two variants.

An ordinary AM radio turns SSB into unintelligible "Donald Duck" audio. A radio with SSB (or a BFO) lets you tune it properly. Tuning AM broadcasts in SSB mode, called ECSS, can also reduce fading distortion.

s: A receiver oscillator that reinserts a carrier so SSB and Morse code become readable.
b: A BFO mixes a locally generated tone with the incoming signal. For CW (Morse) it makes the on/off carrier audible as a tone; for SSB it replaces the missing carrier so speech sounds natural. Older radios have a BFO knob; modern ones handle this in their SSB mode.

s: An AM demodulation method that locks to the carrier, reducing fading distortion and adjacent-channel interference.
b:
A synchronous detector regenerates the station's carrier and locks onto it. This keeps audio stable when selective fading weakens the received carrier. Many sync detectors also let you choose one sideband, so you can avoid interference from a station on one side.

It is one of the most useful features on a shortwave portable.

s: The width of the slice of spectrum a receiver lets through; narrower cuts interference, wider sounds better.
b:
Receivers filter the signal at the intermediate frequency (IF). A wide setting (6 kHz or more on AM) gives fuller audio. A narrow setting (2–3 kHz) cuts interference from nearby stations at the cost of muffled audio. SSB typically uses 2–3 kHz; CW can go below 1 kHz.

Several selectable bandwidths are a good sign on a shortwave radio.

s: How weak a signal a receiver can detect, usually given in microvolts (µV).
b: Sensitivity measures the smallest signal that produces usable audio. Lower numbers are better. In practice most modern portables are sensitive enough; on shortwave, external noise often limits reception before the receiver does, and a better antenna helps more than a more sensitive radio.

s: How well a receiver separates a wanted station from others on nearby frequencies.
b: Good selectivity lets you hear a weak station 5 kHz away from a strong one. It depends on the receiver's filters (bandwidth settings) and design. Selectable bandwidths and sideband-selectable sync both improve practical selectivity.

s: A receiver's ability to handle strong and weak signals at the same time without distortion.
b:
When very strong signals reach a receiver, a radio with limited dynamic range overloads and produces false signals ("phantoms") across the band. This is common with long outdoor antennas on cheap radios or 8-bit SDRs.

An attenuator, a shorter antenna or a receiver with better dynamic range fixes it.

s: A receiver that demodulates and filters signals digitally, often on a single chip.
b:
DSP (digital signal processing) radios convert the signal to digital form and do filtering and demodulation in software. Single-chip receivers such as Silicon Labs' Si47xx series and NXP's TEF6686 made capable portables cheap.

DSP gives clean filters and stable tuning, but chip-based designs vary: some lack SSB, and some mute briefly while tuning ("soft mute").

s: A receiver that digitises a wide slice of spectrum and does the rest in computer software.
b:
An SDR sends raw radio data to a computer, phone or tablet, where software tunes, filters and demodulates it. You can see a whole band at once on a waterfall display and switch modes freely.

Entry-level options like the RTL-SDR Blog V4 cost around $30; HF-focused designs such as the Airspy HF+ Discovery and SDRplay RSPdx-R2 offer better shortwave performance.

s: Internet-connected receivers you can tune from a web browser.
b: WebSDR and KiwiSDR are networks of receivers run by volunteers. Open one in a browser and tune it as if it were your own radio, hearing the band from that location. They are useful for listening without a radio, checking whether a station is on air, or hearing a signal from its target area.

s: A scrolling spectrum display that shows signals as lines over time.
b: SDR software shows a spectrum graph and, under it, a waterfall: each new line is the current spectrum, colour-coded by strength, with older lines scrolling down. Steady carriers show as solid lines, Morse as dashes and digital modes as distinctive patterns, so you can spot activity before you tune it.

s: A single length of wire connected to a receiver's antenna input; the simplest outdoor antenna.
b:
A longwire is any length of wire, ideally outdoors and as high as practical, connected to the radio's external antenna jack. Even 5–10 m out a window usually beats a telescopic whip.

For best results use an unun and a ground, keep the wire away from household wiring, and avoid lengths near a half wavelength on the bands you care about.

s: A wire antenna cut into two equal halves, fed in the centre; resonant on a chosen frequency.
b: A half-wave dipole is two equal wires fed in the middle with coax. Total length in feet is about 468 divided by the frequency in MHz (142.6 ÷ MHz for metres). Cut for one band, it works best there, though for receiving it also performs reasonably on others.

s: A wire loop antenna, often compact, that can reduce local noise and null interference by rotating.
b:
Small loop antennas respond mainly to the magnetic part of a signal, which makes them less sensitive to nearby electrical noise. They are directional, so rotating them can null an interfering station or noise source.

Active loops add an amplifier; passive designs such as tuned MW loops need none.

s: A compact antenna with a built-in amplifier.
b: Active antennas use a short element plus an amplifier to deliver a usable signal where a long wire won't fit. Good ones work well in apartments; poor ones add noise or overload the receiver. Placement away from household electronics matters more than the amplifier.

s: Transformers that match an antenna to a feed line; a 9:1 unun is common for longwires.
b: A balun connects a balanced antenna (like a dipole) to unbalanced coax. An unun connects an unbalanced antenna (like a longwire) to coax. A 9:1 unun brings the high impedance of a random wire closer to 50 Ω, so you can run coax from the antenna to the radio and keep the noisy indoor section out of the antenna.

s: Electrical noise from household devices that drowns out weak shortwave signals.
b:
Switching power supplies, LED lights, solar inverters, TVs and routers all radiate noise across the shortwave bands. In towns this local noise is often the main limit on reception.

Find sources by switching breakers off one at a time while listening on battery power. Move the antenna outdoors and away from the house, or try a loop.

s: A shortwave station that broadcasts strings of numbers, letters or tones, widely believed to carry coded messages to agents.
b: Numbers stations transmit spoken digits, phonetic letters, Morse or data, usually on a schedule, with no station identification. They are generally believed to send one-time-pad messages to intelligence officers. Several remain active and can be heard on ordinary radios.

s: Non-broadcast shortwave users: aviation, maritime, military, weather fax and similar services.
b: Utility stations transmit for a purpose other than public broadcasting. Examples include aviation weather (VOLMET), oceanic air-traffic control, coast guard and maritime stations, weather fax and military networks. Most use SSB or digital modes, so an SSB-capable receiver is needed.

s: Unlicensed broadcasters, often hobbyists, usually heard on weekend evenings.
b: Shortwave pirates are unlicensed stations, often run by hobbyists with modest power. In North America many are heard around 6.9 MHz (43 m) on weekend evenings; in Europe, around 6.2 MHz and in the upper part of the 48 m band. They tend to appear irregularly.

s: A station that broadcasts precise time ticks and announcements, such as WWV.
b: Time signal stations transmit continuous ticks and voice or coded time from atomic clocks. WWV (Colorado) transmits on 2.5, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 MHz; WWVH (Hawaii) on 2.5, 5, 10 and 15 MHz. CHU in Canada uses 3330, 7850 and 14670 kHz. They are also handy for checking which bands are open.

s: Deliberate interference transmitted to block reception of a station.
b: Some governments transmit noise, tones or competing audio on the frequencies of broadcasters they want to block. Jamming was widespread during the Cold War and still targets some broadcasts today. Jammers often appear as a roaring or bubbling noise on the frequency.

s: A transmitter site that rebroadcasts another country's or organisation's programmes closer to the target area.
b: Broadcasters often lease time on transmitters in other countries to get a better path to their audience. Schedules list the transmitter site, so the same station can be heard from several locations through the day.

s: The output power of a broadcast transmitter, typically 100–500 kW for major international stations.
b: International broadcasters commonly use 100–300 kW, and some sites run 500 kW. Higher power helps, but antenna direction and propagation matter more: a 100 kW signal beamed at you can beat a 500 kW signal aimed elsewhere.

s: Numbered geographic zones used to describe where a shortwave broadcast is aimed.
b: Broadcasters and the HFCC describe target areas using CIRAF zones, a numbered grid of the world. Schedules such as EIBI translate these into regions like "NAm" (North America) or "Eu" (Europe). A broadcast beamed at your area is usually easier to hear.

s: A digital broadcasting standard for shortwave, mediumwave and longwave that gives near-FM audio quality.
b: DRM packs digital audio and data into a normal shortwave channel. When reception is good, audio is clean and free of fading noise; when it is too weak, it drops out completely. A DRM receiver or an SDR with DRM decoding software is needed.

s: Continuous wave: on/off keying of a carrier, used to send Morse code.
b: CW is the oldest radio mode: the transmitter's carrier is switched on and off in the dots and dashes of Morse code. It is narrow and gets through weak conditions. To hear it as a tone you need a BFO or SSB/CW mode.

s: Text and data modes such as radioteletype, decoded with software from the receiver's audio.
b: RTTY (radioteletype) shifts between two tones to send text. Other digital modes include weather fax, FT8 and various data systems. Feed the receiver's audio (in SSB mode) to free decoding software on a computer or phone.

s: The 120 m, 90 m and 60 m bands (about 2.3–5.1 MHz), used for domestic broadcasting in tropical regions.
b: These low shortwave bands were allocated for domestic broadcasting in the tropics, where static makes mediumwave hard. Signals are weak and mainly heard at night, which makes them a DX challenge. Many tropical-band stations have closed, but a few remain.
